title: How to Get Doctors to Take You Seriously About Gut Symptoms
summary: Prepare dated evidence and clear questions so your gut symptoms get a fair look.
body_markdown:
Months of diarrhea, cramping or blood in the toilet can be hard to explain in a short appointment, and many people leave feeling brushed aside. Clinicians weigh many possible causes at once, and the details they hear shape what they test. Learning how to get doctors to take you seriously about gut symptoms is mostly preparation: specific, dated information, questions about the clinician's reasoning, and a confirmed plan. This guide draws on research about diagnostic delay in Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis (UC) and offers phrases you can use at your next visit, whether you are the patient or the person helping them.


## Why gut symptoms get dismissed


Diagnostic delay in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is well documented. A[meta-analysis of 101 studies covering 112,194 patients worldwide](https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10163245/1/Systematic%20review%20with%20meta%20analysis.pdf) found a median of median times from first symptoms to diagnosis of 8.0 months for Crohn's disease and 3.7 months for UC, or 6.2 and 3.2 months in high-income countries. The same review linked delay, defined as falling above the 75th centile of time to diagnosis, to higher odds of strictures, penetrating disease and intestinal surgery in Crohn's, and of colectomy in UC.


Early IBD symptoms overlap with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). In[UK primary-care records from 1998 to 2016](https://openaccess.sgul.ac.uk/id/eprint/112110) , fewer than half of people later diagnosed with IBD who had chronic gut symptoms saw a specialist within 18 months, and a prior IBS or depression diagnosis was linked to slower review. UK referral rules differ from many US plans, so these figures may not translate directly.


A[study of 190 patients at four hospitals in Valencia, Spain](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10697413/) found women waited a median 12.6 months for a Crohn's diagnosis versus 4.5 months for men, and were more often misdiagnosed with a functional gut disorder. The gap arose after women entered care. These regional figures are not US rates.


None of this makes an IBS diagnosis wrong. The[American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) IBS guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33315591/) favors a positive diagnostic strategy, and IBS is common and real. Persistent symptoms, warning signs or a poor response to treatment still justify another look.


## Before the visit: turn symptoms into evidence


[MedlinePlus advice on talking with your doctor](https://medlineplus.gov/talkingwithyourdoctor.html) suggests writing down your questions, listing every medicine and supplement, and describing when symptoms started and what makes them better or worse. For gut symptoms, a few weeks of notes usually tell a clearer story than memory.


Focus on change over time. "Since March I go six to eight times a day, up from once, and twice a night" gives a clinician far more to work with than "my stomach is bad." A one-page summary covers three areas:


- A timeline of what changed, with approximate dates
- Two to four weeks of daily notes on stool frequency, blood, urgency, pain and whether symptoms wake you
- Weight readings, treatments already tried with their results, and copies of earlier test results


Record anything[NIDDK lists as a reason for further evaluation](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/irritable-bowel-syndrome/diagnosis) , including rectal bleeding, black or tarry stools, weight loss, anemia, and a family history of celiac disease, colon cancer or IBD. A guide to[the differences between IBS and IBD and the red flags doctors watch for](https://aidyhq.com/learn/ibs-vs-ibd-key-differences-red-flags-and-the-tests-doctors-use) can help you decide what belongs on the page.


## In the room: what to say


Open with what changed and how it affects your life, since that is the information a short visit can lose. You might say, "My bowel habits changed four months ago, and I now plan every outing around bathrooms. I have also lost eight pounds without trying."


If you are given a likely explanation, asking about the reasoning is a fair request. Useful questions include:


- "What else could this be, and what makes you think it is less likely?"
- "What would make you want to test for IBD or another cause?"
- "If this treatment does not help, what is the next step, and when?"


These questions invite the clinician's reasoning without challenging their expertise and create checkpoints for the next visit.


Mention any relative with IBD, celiac disease or colon cancer, since[NIDDK names family history as prompting further testing](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/digestive-diseases/irritable-bowel-syndrome/diagnosis) . If you have been told your symptoms are stress, you can agree stress may play a part and still ask what has been ruled out.


## Asking about specific tests without demanding them


You can ask about tests while respecting that the clinician decides what is appropriate. The[ACG IBS guideline](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33315591/) suggests checking fecal calprotectin, a stool test, in people with suspected IBS and diarrhea to rule out IBD, and serologic testing to rule out celiac disease. If those apply to you, a question might sound like, "I read that a stool calprotectin test is sometimes used to help rule out IBD when diarrhea is the main symptom. Would that be useful for me, or is there a reason it does not fit?"


The same approach works for a referral. "Given how long this has gone on, would it help for me to see a gastroenterologist?" is a fair question in primary care. If you already see one and suspect IBD, a guide to[finding an IBD specialist](https://aidyhq.com/learn/how-to-find-an-ibd-specialist-not-just-a-general-gastroenterologist) explains what that extra training covers.


Direct-to-consumer microbiome or food-sensitivity kits are a poor basis for this conversation. Asking how a recommended test would change the plan is more productive, and a normal result is still useful information.


## Before you leave: confirm the plan


Restating the plan in your own words is a simple way to catch misunderstandings. In clinical settings this is called teach-back, and a[systematic review of 20 studies, nine of them randomized trials](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7156054/) found it was effective in 19 of them for outcomes such as knowledge, self-care and adherence. Those studies tested teach-back led by clinicians or research staff. Starting it yourself, with a line such as "Let me repeat the plan back to make sure I have it," is a reasonable adaptation, though it has not been studied directly.


[MedlinePlus](https://medlineplus.gov/talkingwithyourdoctor.html) also suggests taking notes, asking questions until you understand, requesting written instructions, and finding out how to reach your provider afterward. Before you leave, confirm what happens next, when results should arrive, and which changes should prompt an earlier call.


If you agreed to wait and see, you can politely ask that the reasoning and review point be noted in your record, which helps any later clinician see what was considered.


## When to get a second opinion or change doctors


Some symptoms should not wait for a routine follow-up, however your last appointment went.[MedlinePlus advises getting medical help right away](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003120.htm) for sudden sharp abdominal pain, a rigid or tender belly, vomiting blood or blood in the stool, or being unable to pass stool, especially with vomiting. For diarrhea, it advises[contacting a provider right away](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003126.htm) for a fever above 101°F, black stools, or blood or pus in the stool. Nighttime symptoms, unintentional weight loss and anemia are also[described as red flags in IBS evaluation](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5210026/) .


Outside urgent situations, a second opinion makes sense when symptoms continue despite treatment, when the plan still does not make sense after you ask, or when communication has broken down. A guide to[getting a second opinion for Crohn's or UC](https://aidyhq.com/learn/getting-a-second-opinion-for-crohns-or-uc-when-it-helps-and-how-to-prepare) covers how to prepare and what records to bring.


[Medicare Part B covers a second opinion](https://www.medicare.gov/coverage/second-surgical-opinions) for medically necessary, non-emergency surgery, plus a third if the first two differ, at 20% of the approved amount after the deductible. Rules for other second opinions and for private plans differ, so check with your plan before booking.


## If you are advocating for someone else


Partners, parents and friends often notice things the patient has stopped mentioning, such as nighttime bathroom trips, skipped meals or weight change.[MedlinePlus suggests bringing a trusted friend or family member](https://medlineplus.gov/talkingwithyourdoctor.html) to appointments and having them take notes.


Agree on roles beforehand. The patient usually speaks first, and the companion adds observations, keeps the timeline, and asks any planned question that gets missed. A statement like "I have seen him get up three times a night for the past month" adds detail without speaking over the patient. Ask the clinic what permission it needs for you to receive information or call on the patient's behalf.


For patients and companions alike, the approach is the same: specific dated evidence, clear questions about reasoning, a confirmed plan, and prompt action on warning signs. Those habits give clinicians what they need to make good decisions and leave you with a fair record of what was considered, whether the answer turns out to be IBS, IBD or something else.


This article is for educational purposes and is not medical advice. It is researched against current AGA clinical guidelines and peer-reviewed sources. Always discuss treatment decisions with your care team.
